summary: Describes how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can detect data-plane failures on MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs). BFD needs less processing than LSP Ping, so combining them allows faster detection or more paths to be watched. The document explains how the two fit together and gives procedures for using BFD in this setting.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5884 explains how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can monitor an MPLS Label Switched Path for data-plane failures. LSP Ping starts the BFD session and still checks that the path matches the control plane.

subtitle: Use BFD to detect data-plane failures along an MPLS label-switched path.

tldr.problem: An MPLS control plane can remain functional while the data path drops or mis-forwards packets, and LSP Ping can be costly for frequent checks.
tldr.mechanism: LSP Ping starts a BFD session for an LSP and exchanges discriminators; BFD then sends control packets along the same path for failure detection.
tldr.outcome: BFD offers lightweight, fast data-plane monitoring, while LSP Ping remains necessary for checking that the data plane matches the control plane.

today: RFC 5884 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 1122. It is later updated by RFC 7726.

sections.title: Why Monitor the MPLS Data Path
sections.content:
An MPLS path can be mis-forwarding or dropping user traffic even while its control plane appears to work. LSP Ping can detect failures and compare control-plane and data-plane forwarding, but its control-plane processing is relatively expensive.

BFD control packets require less processing and can support faster checks or checks on more paths. BFD cannot verify that the path is mapped to the same Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) at both ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The network needs to check the path that carries packets, not only the routing information that describes it. BFD checks liveness cheaply; LSP Ping checks additional path details.

sections.title: BFD Works Alongside LSP Ping
sections.content:
A BFD session is established for the MPLS LSP being checked. Its control packets travel along the same data path and are processed by the egress Label Switching Router (LSR). A separate session should be established for each FEC when one LSP is associated with multiple FECs.

LSP Ping bootstraps the session and can periodically verify the control plane against the data plane. BFD then exchanges frequent fault-detection packets; the LSP Ping interval should be much less frequent.
sections.plainLanguage: LSP Ping first identifies the path and starts BFD. BFD checks the path repeatedly, while occasional LSP Ping tests confirm that forwarding still matches the intended route.

sections.title: Starting and Identifying a BFD Session
sections.content:
The ingress LSR sends an LSP Ping Echo request containing its local BFD discriminator. If the egress validates the FEC, it returns a BFD control packet that uses that discriminator to identify the session. The egress can also return its own discriminator in the LSP Ping reply.

Once the session is up, each endpoint uses the other endpoint's discriminator to demultiplex BFD packets. The discriminator TLV in LSP Ping has type 15 and carries a 4-byte local discriminator.
sections.plainLanguage: LSP Ping carries each router's BFD identifier so both ends can match later BFD packets to the right path. The identifier tells the receiver which session the packet belongs to.

sections.title: Encapsulating BFD Control Packets
sections.content:
The ingress sends BFD control packets in the MPLS label stack for the FEC under test. The packet is UDP, with destination port 3784, a routable source address, and an IP TTL or hop limit of 1.

The egress can route its reply using UDP destination port 4784 or return it through an MPLS label stack using destination port 3784. Once the session is up, endpoints must not change their source address or local discriminator without first bringing the session down.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD packets follow the MPLS path being checked and use fixed UDP destination ports. The routers keep their session identifiers stable while the session remains up.

sections.title: Failure Detection and Fast Reroute
sections.content:
If the BFD detection interval is shorter than an MPLS fast-reroute switchover, BFD may declare a failure while traffic is moving to a backup path. The interval should therefore be longer than the switchover time.

The security guidance from BFD, LSP Ping, and the relevant MPLS specifications also applies. Routed replies should follow the authentication guidance for multihop BFD.
sections.plainLanguage: A very short BFD timer can mistake a planned path switch for a failure. Set the detection interval with the backup-path switchover time in mind.
